prompt.context: Your client is Idaho Johnson, an archeologist/adventurer who specializes in rare artifact recovery. They have just learned about the possibility of an incredibly valuable 6,000 year old crown buried in the Siwa Oasis of Northwestern Egypt. You have been hired to determine whether Idaho should launch an expedition to recover this artifact.
prompt.question: Should Idaho Johnson launch an expedition to recover the artifact? Walk me through your analysis.

clarifying_info.q: How will the expedition be financed?
clarifying_info.a: He must self-finance the dig, but he finds a buyer ahead of time and strikes the deal pending the recovery.

clarifying_info.q: How did he learn about the artifact?
clarifying_info.a: A colleague came to him with a map she is willing to sell to him.
He is currently located in Indiana.

clarifying_info.q: How long will the dig take?
clarifying_info.a: The dig is estimated to take one year (12 months).
He only wants to go on the expedition if he can make an expected ROI of 85%.

clarifying_info.q: What is the probability of successfully retrieving the artifact?
clarifying_info.a: He believes he has a 20% chance of success.
He has some equipment but would need to buy more for this expedition.

exhibits.title: Expedition Costs
exhibits.shows: A table listing cost categories and their associated amounts for the expedition.

data.Note: Travel cost listed is only for one direction of travel; Idaho plus 5 employees = 6 people traveling

framework: Costs: Break into one-time costs (travel, map, equipment, legal/permits), recurring costs (labor wages, food/lodging), and opportunity costs (teaching salary foregone)
Artifact Value: Determine revenue from selling the artifact — compare one-time sale vs. recurring revenue stream; calculate PV if recurring
Risks: Probability of success (20%), competition finding artifact first, personal danger, self-financing risk
Alternatives: Other artifacts, safer expeditions, film franchise, selling the map itself

questions.prompt: What costs would be required to embark on this expedition? Bucket them into categories.
questions.guidance: A strong answer organizes costs into three buckets: (1) Upfront/one-time costs: map, travel, legal/permits/visa/vaccines, equipment. (2) Recurring costs: labor (workers' wages), lodging, food. (3) Opportunity costs: teaching salary foregone, other potential expeditions missed.

questions.prompt: Calculate the total cost of this expedition using the exhibit provided.
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the exhibit data to each bucket. Clarify if asked: food/lodging figure is for the entire group. Travel is one direction so must be doubled.

math.setup: One-time costs = Map/Equipment + Legal + Travel (round-trip for 6 people). Recurring costs = Labor + Food/Lodging over 12 months. Opportunity cost = Missed salary.

questions.prompt: There are two buyers: a private collector offering a one-time payment of $4M, and the Beelong Zynna Museum offering a share of exhibit ticket revenue. How would you practically calculate the value of the museum's offer, and which offer is better?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize the museum offer is a perpetuity (or growing perpetuity) and calculate its present value. Strong candidates identify that you would benchmark against comparable museums (size, urban location, similar artifacts) to project visitor and ticket data. The PV formula for a growing perpetuity is PV = CF / (r - g).

math.setup: Museum Attendance = 900,000/yr; % purchasing exhibit ticket = 50%; Ticket price = $10; Explorer's share = 10%; Discount rate = 15%; Growth rate = 5%.
steps: Compare: Museum offer PV ($4.5M) > Private collector offer ($4M)
math.answer: Museum deal is worth $4.5M in PV terms, which is better than the $4M one-time payment from the private collector.

questions.prompt: Given that Idaho has a 20% chance of successfully retrieving the artifact, what is the expected ROI? Should he go?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate expected revenue using probability-weighted outcomes, then compute ROI against total cost. Key insight: even though expected revenue exceeds opportunity cost alone, the ROI falls just short of the 85% threshold Idaho requires. A nuanced candidate will flag this is close and weigh qualitative factors.

math.setup: Success probability = 20%; Revenue on success = $4.5M (museum deal); Revenue on failure = $0; Total cost = $500,000; Required ROI = 85%.
steps: Compare to required ROI: 80% < 85% — just below the threshold
math.answer: Expected ROI is 80%, which falls short of Idaho's required 85% ROI threshold.

brainstorming.prompt: What costs would be required to embark on this expedition? Brainstorm and bucket your answer.

recommendation: Based purely on the numbers, the expected ROI is 80%, which falls just short of Idaho's required 85% threshold — the financial case is borderline against proceeding.
However, the shortfall is small (5 percentage points) and several upside factors could push actual returns above the threshold.
risks: ROI (80%) is below the required threshold of 85%
Only a 20% chance of successfully retrieving the artifact
Self-financed expedition means Idaho bears full personal financial risk
Museum revenue projections may be incorrect or lower than modeled
Significant personal danger associated with the expedition
Competitors could find the artifact first
next_steps: If Go: Plan the expedition in detail; assemble a crew; gather remaining supplies; book charter transport to Egypt; secure map purchase; lock in museum agreement in writing

If No Go: Identify other artifacts or revenue opportunities with better risk-adjusted returns; continue teaching and collect salary; explore buying and reselling the map for profit without mounting the full expedition
